title: Ayushmann Khurrana's 'Pati Patni Aur Woh Do' Crosses ₹24 Crore — Is Bollywood's Mid-Budget Comedy Back?
excerpt: The rom-com sequel has quietly become the 8th highest-grossing Bollywood film of 2026, proving that star power plus relatable storytelling still fills theatres
body:
In a year dominated by ₹100 crore blockbusters and franchise sequels, a mid-budget rom-com has quietly reminded Bollywood of something important: you don't always need spectacle to sell tickets. Sometimes, you just need Ayushmann Khurrana being extremely Ayushmann Khurrana.

Pati Patni Aur Woh Do, the sequel to the 2019 hit (itself a remake of the 1978 Sanjeev Kumar classic), has crossed ₹24 crore net in India in its first four days, earning its spot as the 8th highest-grossing Bollywood film of 2026. The worldwide gross stands at approximately ₹33 crore, with overseas markets contributing a solid ₹4 crore.

The Box Office Play-by-Play

The film opened on Thursday, May 15 with a modest ₹4.38 crore — not earth-shattering, but respectable for a film without action-hero spectacle. Then Saturday happened: ₹5.75 crore, a 50% spike that signaled strong word-of-mouth. Sunday delivered the knockout punch at ₹7.75 crore — a remarkable 106% increase over opening day — as family audiences turned out for afternoon and evening screenings.

Monday's hold at ₹3.25-3.50 crore is the crucial number. A 50% drop from Sunday is standard physics for any Bollywood release, and the film's weekday trajectory suggests it has legs. Industry analysts are projecting a lifetime collection of ₹40-50 crore — solid profit territory for a film at this budget.

The Cast and the Comedy

Directed by Mudassar Aziz (who also helmed the first installment), the sequel stars Khurrana as Prajapati, a man juggling complications with three women played by Sara Ali Khan, Rakul Preet Singh, and Wamiqa Gabbi. The comedy-of-errors premise — part situational farce, part commentary on modern relationships — has drawn comparisons to classic Hindi cinema's screwball tradition.

Critical reception has been mixed. Some reviewers praised Khurrana's comic timing and the film's breezy first half; others found the plot thin and the sequel unnecessary. But audiences have spoken with their BookMyShow taps: the film cracked 690,000 ticket sales on a single day, becoming one of the platform's top-selling Hindi films of the month.

Why NRIs Are Watching

For diaspora audiences, Bollywood comedies have always been comfort food — the cinematic equivalent of calling home. Pati Patni Aur Woh Do taps into relationship dynamics that NRIs recognize: the arranged-marriage expectations, the family judgments, the gap between how you present your relationship to parents and how it actually works.

The film's overseas performance — ₹4 crore in four days, with Bengaluru and US metro audiences leading the charge — suggests it's finding its natural audience among younger NRIs who grew up on Ayushmann's brand of intelligent, slightly awkward everyman comedy. It's not Dhurandhar 2 money (nothing is — that film's ₹1,183 crore is in a different galaxy), but it doesn't need to be.

The Bigger Picture

What makes PPAWD's performance noteworthy isn't the raw numbers — it's what the numbers represent. Bollywood in 2026 has been a story of extremes: mega-budget tentpoles that either break records or break studios, with very little middle ground. This film's steady, word-of-mouth-driven climb is a reminder that the ₹40-50 crore mid-range hit — the bread and butter of Hindi cinema for decades — isn't dead. It just needs the right star, the right genre, and the right price point.

Ayushmann Khurrana, who built his career on exactly this formula (Vicky Donor, Badhaai Ho, Dream Girl), remains one of the few Bollywood actors who can reliably open a non-franchise, non-action film to respectable numbers.

What's Next

The second week is make-or-break. Drishyam 3 arrives on Wednesday, and the competition for screens will intensify. But PPAWD has already proven its theatrical viability. The OTT window (likely 6-8 weeks post-release) will extend its reach to NRI audiences who missed it in theatres — and for a comedy this rewatchable, the streaming afterlife could be substantial.
